finding: Income and CO2 per person rise together across countries
corroborated_by: Week 1 preliminary smoke test; Week 3 income per person is the strongest model feature

finding: CO2 per person differs across the four income groups
corroborated_by: Week 3 decoupling windows differ sharply by income group

finding: High-income countries emit far more per person than lower-income countries
corroborated_by: Week 3 decoupling windows differ sharply by income group

finding: The income-emissions slope is flatter in high-income countries
corroborated_by: none: no other week tests slopes
why: 2 of 6 robustness variants do not reach raw p < 0.05; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0155 (not below 0.01); not corroborated by another week

finding: CO2 per person fell in high-income countries between 1990 and 2022
corroborated_by: Week 3 high-income windows keep decoupling in 2017-2019
why: Holm-adjusted p = 0.0155 (not below 0.01); observed effect size is below the minimum detectable effect (0.29) flagged in Week 2

finding: Absolute decoupling is far more common in high-income countries
corroborated_by: Week 3 window base rates rise steadily with income group

finding: Industry share (not urbanisation) adds explanatory power beyond income (exploratory)
corroborated_by: Week 3 industry share has the expected sign but urbanisation disagrees
why: exploratory, outside the confirmatory family; not corroborated by another week

finding: The selected model ranks decoupling windows better than the persistence rule
corroborated_by: rolling-origin cross-validation (an earlier period) shows the same ordering
why: paired interval excludes zero and both variants agree, but the gain is modest, there is a single COVID-shaped test period, and a free income-group base rate scores about the same (post hoc)

finding: At the frozen threshold the selected model is not useful as a yes/no classifier
corroborated_by: the same pattern appears in out-of-fold cross-validation (Week 3, Section 8.3)
why: no usefulness threshold was pre-specified, so the judgement rests on MCC and precision against the base rate; test MCC 0.072, precision 0.254

finding: An income-group base rate scores about as well as the selected model
why: post hoc: added after the test set was seen

finding: Random forest and boosting score higher than the selected model on the test set
corroborated_by: cross-validation also ranked the forest first (but within one standard error)
why: post hoc; the pre-specified choice was not changed

finding: Precision among the highest-scored windows exceeds the base rate
why: new in Week 4, computed after the test set was seen; plain-language aid only

finding: Structural drivers (industry share, fuel mix) matter beyond income; urbanisation does not clearly
corroborated_by: partly: Week 3 oil share and industry share carry signal, but urbanisation is inconsistent
why: Week 2's test was exploratory (unadjusted p), Week 3 importance is predictive not causal, and urbanisation results disagree across weeks

finding: Data lineage can be checked, and was: same OWID file, identical World Bank values, one checksum test failing on line endings
why: observed directly and verified by src/lineage.py; no inference involved

finding: Headline numbers carry wide or fragile intervals that a bare number would hide
why: observed in the saved results and recomputed independently

finding: Week 1's preliminary rank correlation between income and CO2 per person
why: a planning-stage smoke test, not a result of the exploratory analysis; used only as a consistency check
